title: Chapter VIII
focus: injustice and the burden of silence

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “I did confess; but I confessed a lie” slowly and put it in my own words: Justine, condemned for William's murder, tells Elizabeth she falsely confessed because her confessor threatened her with damnation. Next, craft. I notice the paradox of confessing a lie, which turns a religious act into a tool of injustice. The strongest word is “lie”: it shows the confession that condemned her was forced and false. Then, effect. What does Justine mean when she says she confessed a lie? My answer: Justine dies innocent while Victor, who knows the truth, stays silent; her false confession exposes how fear and authority can crush the innocent.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.
